title: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second one. Solve it in a single pass. (LeetCode: Middle of the Linked List)
shortTitle: Middle of the LinkedList (Fast and Slow Pointers)

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the middle of a linked list uses two pointers where a fast pointer advances two nodes for every one node the slow pointer advances. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. For an even-length list this returns the second of the two middle nodes, and it completes in a single pass with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked statement pages and wants the middle page without first counting how many there are. He sends a slow walker that steps one page at a time and a fast walker that steps two pages at a time. By the time the fast walker reaches the last page, the slow walker is standing exactly on the middle page. No counting, no second trip through the chain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fast moves two, slow moves one; when fast hits the end, slow is the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the middle of a linked list uses two pointers where a fast pointer advances two nodes for every one node the slow pointer advances. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. For an even-length list this returns the second of the two middle nodes, and it completes in a single pass with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked statement pages and wants the middle page without first counting how many there are. He sends a slow walker that steps one page at a time and a fast walker that steps two pages at a time. By the time the fast walker reaches the last page, the slow walker is standing exactly on the middle page. No counting, no second trip through the chain.

**One line to remember:** Fast moves two, slow moves one; when fast hits the end, slow is the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach walks the list once to count the nodes, computes the middle index, then walks again to reach it, which is two passes. The two-pointer approach does it in a single pass using the speed ratio.

We start both a slow and a fast pointer at the head. In each iteration we move slow one node forward and fast two nodes forward. The loop continues while fast is not null and fast.next is not null. When the loop ends, the fast pointer has either reached the end or stepped just past it, and because fast moved twice as fast, the slow pointer has covered exactly half the distance, so it sits on the middle node.

For an odd-length list the middle is unambiguous and slow lands on it. For an even-length list there are two middle candidates, and this formulation returns the second one, because the loop condition lets fast advance one extra time. If the problem required the first of two middles, we would stop one step earlier by changing the loop condition.

A finance usage example: suppose statement pages are linked as `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4 -> P5`. Slow visits P1, P2, P3, and fast visits P1, P3, P5. When fast reaches P5, its next is null, so the loop stops and slow is at P3, the middle. For an even list `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4`, slow ends at P3, the second middle.

The senior-level nuance: the exact loop condition determines whether you get the first or second middle on even-length lists, and interviewers often probe this, so stating the convention explicitly matters. This fast-slow pattern is a building block for many list problems, including detecting the midpoint before reversing the second half for a palindrome check or for reordering a list. The single-pass property is the main advantage over the count-then-walk approach, especially when the list is large or when you cannot traverse it twice cheaply.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India links a customer's monthly statement pages into a chain, and a rendering feature needs to jump directly to the middle page to show a quick summary split point. Counting all the pages first and then walking again to the middle is two passes over what can be a very long chain, which the rendering service wants to avoid for latency reasons.

Problem 2 — When the number of pages is even, the product requirement is to land on the second of the two middle pages, so the algorithm's convention must match that requirement exactly.

The code defines a `StatementNavigator` class with a `findMiddle` method implementing the fast-slow pointer technique. A runnable demo builds an odd-length and an even-length page chain and logs the middle page in each.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an odd chain `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4 -> P5` and an even chain `P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4`.

Step 1: For the odd chain, slow and fast both start at P1. The loop checks fast and fast.next are not null, which holds.

Step 2: Slow moves to P2 and fast moves to P3. The loop checks again: fast is P3, fast.next is P4, both non-null.

Step 3: Slow moves to P3 and fast moves to P5. Now fast.next is null, so the loop exits and slow is at P3, the exact middle of the five pages.

Step 4: For the even chain, slow and fast start at P1. Slow moves to P2 and fast moves to P3. The loop checks: fast is P3, fast.next is P4, non-null.

Step 5: Slow moves to P3 and fast moves two steps to null. The loop exits with slow at P3, which is the second of the two middle pages P2 and P3, matching the required convention.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:05:00 PM com.bank.statement.StatementNavDemo main
INFO: Middle page = P3
INFO: Odd middle: P3
INFO: Middle page = P3
INFO: Even middle: P3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ODD: P1→P2→P3→P4→P5
    slow: P1→P2→P3
    fast: P1→P3→P5 (next null) → stop
    middle = P3

  EVEN: P1→P2→P3→P4
    slow: P1→P2→P3
    fast: P1→P3→null → stop
    middle = P3 (second of P2/P3)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the middle node of a singly linked list is the classic fast-slow pointer problem, and the whole point is to do it in a single pass rather than counting the nodes first and then walking again. I start a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, and on each step I move the slow pointer forward one node and the fast pointer forward two nodes.

The arithmetic is simple: because the fast pointer covers twice the distance of the slow pointer, by the time the fast pointer reaches the end of the list the slow pointer has covered exactly half, so it sits on the middle node. I keep the loop running while the fast pointer and its next are both non-null. For an odd-length list the middle is unambiguous and the slow pointer lands right on it. For an even-length list there are two middle candidates, and this particular loop condition returns the second one, because it lets the fast pointer take one extra step; if the requirement were the first of the two middles, I would stop one step earlier by tightening the loop condition.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a statement viewer. We linked a customer's monthly statement pages into a chain, and a feature needed to jump straight to the middle page to show a summary split point. Counting all the pages and then walking again was two passes over a potentially long chain, which hurt latency, so the single-pass fast-slow technique gave us the middle directly. Our product requirement was to land on the second of the two middle pages for even-length statements, which matched this formulation exactly.

The senior-level point I make is that the precise loop condition determines first-versus-second middle on even-length lists, and interviewers very often probe this, so I always state the convention explicitly rather than leaving it implicit. I also note that this fast-slow midpoint is a foundational building block: it is the first step in checking whether a list is a palindrome, in reordering a list, and in splitting a list into halves, so mastering it cleanly pays off across a whole family of linked list problems.
